reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The .409 xwOBA and 2.69 xERA live in the same body, which is the whole argument. As a hitter, the contact quality is severe: 93.6 mph average exit velocity, a 15.9% barrel rate, a 15.1% walk rate that gives him an on-base profile most pure hitters can't match, and a projection of .281/.395/.540 over 690 plate attempts reflects that the bat plays even when the strikeout rate sits at 22.8%. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball with 2486 rpm of spin behind a 30.4% whiff rate produces a xERA that sits with the rotation's elite tier. The one thing this profile genuinely hinges on is health, specifically whether he can sustain both workloads across a full Dodger season, because if the pitching side gets shelved again you have a premier DH, and if the bat cools during heavy pitching stretches you have a premier starter, and either version is excellent but neither version is this.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: A 19.1% walk rate sitting alongside a 36.4% whiff rate is the whole tension in Kurtz's profile: he barely chases at 22.6%, draws walks at an elite clip, but when pitchers locate in the zone he swings and misses at a rate that puts him near the bottom of the league. The power underneath it, 94.5 mph average exit velocity and an 18.9% barrel rate, is the kind of raw that makes the strikeouts survivable if the walk rate holds. His .390 xwOBA says the actual production isn't far behind what the batted-ball profile promises, and the projection backs that up with 38 home runs and a .403 OBP across a full season. Everything here hinges on whether pitchers find an in-zone approach that exploits the whiff rate without walking him: if they can, the strikeout number climbs toward unsustainable; if they can't, you're looking at a legitimate middle-of-the-order force at 23.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the one ugly number in an otherwise compelling profile, and it hasn't buried him yet. Crow-Armstrong's hard-hit rate checks in at 50.2%, his xwOBA sits at .365, and the xSLG of .482 suggests the current slugging projection of .499 is honest contact-quality work rather than a flier. The 36.5% chase rate explains the 25.5% strikeout rate, and it's the one dependency: if he never tightens that zone, the floor is a strikeout-heavy power-speed outfielder whose 10.6% walk rate keeps him from becoming a liability, but whose ceiling stays just out of reach. If he does tighten it, a 32-homer, 36-steal season at .853 OPS is not a stretch for a 24-year-old with 29.4 ft/s speed and genuine thump behind the ball.

reports.name: Paul Skenes

A 30.1% strikeout rate with only 5.6% walks is the engine: he's missing bats and almost never giving free passes, a combination that makes a 3.30 ERA projection across a full workload feel conservative rather than generous. The one wrinkle in the Statcast card is the 28.3% whiff rate sitting well below what you'd expect given the strikeout numbers, which suggests the swing-and-miss comes more from command and pitch shape than from pure zone dominance. reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact quality is genuinely elite, 53.0% hard-hit rate and 91.9 mph average exit velocity, but the power hasn't translated the way you'd expect, and that gap is the whole conversation with Tatis right now. His xBA sits at .287, which is as good as almost anyone, yet the xSLG of .435 and a 28.6% whiff rate suggest he's making loud contact without consistently doing damage at the barrel level. The projection lands at .277/.348/.419 with 17 home runs across 700 PA, which for a guy this athletic with 35 projected steals reads less like a superstar line and more like a very good, very fast regular. If the barrel rate climbs and the whiff rate drops, the power catches up to the contact quality and you get something much closer to the guy everyone expected; if it doesn't, you're valuing him almost entirely on average, on-base, and legs.

reports.name: Theo Gillen
reports.peak_summary: Projection: everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is impact over 265 PA.
reports.published_report: A .405 BABIP is the number every scout circles first, and it earns the skepticism. Gillen is hitting .320/.426/.541 across AA and A+ this year, and the BABIP asks whether the contact is genuinely elite or partly a speed-driven mirage, because 30 stolen bases in 312 PA means he's turning singles into extras and pressuring defenses in ways that inflate surface reads. The translation is honest about what survives the jump: the walk rate clears MLB average at 10.4%, the power largely evaporates to a .151 ISO right at league mean, and the strikeout rate climbs to 26% against a 22% MLB baseline, so what looks like an impact bat becomes a hit-tool-and-legs profile at the big-league level. If the hit tool holds, he's an everyday center fielder; if the BABIP regresses hard and the bat-to-ball doesn't survive the upper minors, the floor is a reserve with speed.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report: The speed is the one legitimate separator. At 29.2 ft/s, Lile runs at the 93rd percentile, and that's what keeps 15 projected stolen bases believable and gives the rest of the profile more room to breathe than a cold read of the bat would suggest. The contact numbers are encouraging enough, a 17.0% strikeout rate sitting well above league average, but a 37.1% chase rate and 35.0% hard-hit rate tell you the bat-to-ball efficiency is solid while the thump behind it isn't. His xwOBA of .318 lands at the 45th percentile, which is about what a .737 projected OPS earns you: a fringe regular who plays every day because the glove and the legs make the whole package add up. If the chase rate comes down as he settles in at 23, he pushes toward a useful everyday outfielder; if it stays where it is, he's a good fourth outfielder who steals bases.

reports.name: Elmer Rodríguez
reports.peak_summary: Projection: multi-inning or setup reliever with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 61.3 IP.
reports.published_report: The ERA is doing a lot of heavy lifting here. Rodríguez is running a 2.9 in Triple-A through 61.3 innings, which translates to a run-prevention grade that sits well above the field, but the underlying strikeout and walk numbers tell a different story: his K/9 translates to 8.2 against a big-league average of 8.6, and his walk rate comes out to 4.2 when the MLB average is 3.2. He's keeping runs off the board without missing bats or throwing strikes at a rate that sustains it. If the ERA holds, there's a useful middle-relief arm here, the kind that fills up innings without embarrassing anybody; if the command doesn't sharpen, the whole thing unravels into a depth piece the moment better hitters start making contact.

reports.name: Michael Arroyo
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 292 PA.
reports.published_report: The contact is the carrying tool here. At AA, Arroyo is striking out just 17% of the time, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts that at 20.4% against a league that runs 22.0%, so the bat-to-ball skill doesn't evaporate at the next level the way it does for a lot of prospects. The .289/.366/.461 line across 292 PA isn't a hot streak; the .320 BABIP isn't out of step with what you'd expect from a hitter who makes this much contact, and 13 stolen bases suggest he's doing something with the on-base too. The profile hinges on whether the power holds up, because the MLB-equivalent ISO of .139 slides below average, and a bench bat who can't get to even fringe-average power at the next level is depth rather than a roster piece. Figure him as a platoon second baseman if the hit tool translates and the pop stays close; if the gap between his AA ISO and MLB average widens, the contact alone probably earns him a long career as a reserve.

reports.name: Connelly Early
reports.published_report: The chase rate does real work here — 31.4% gets hitters fishing outside the zone often enough to soften what's otherwise a concerning contact profile. The barrel rate against him sits at 10.6% and average exit velocity is 90.6 mph, both indicating he's giving up hard contact more than you'd want from someone projecting as a rotation piece, and the xERA of 4.30 is probably closer to his true talent level than the 3.66 projection. His K% of 23.8% is functional but the 23.7% whiff rate suggests he's generating chase more than swings-and-misses in the zone, so if that 31.4% chase number drifts back toward league norms, there isn't another weapon in the profile to compensate. Ceiling is a back-end starter eating innings in a Boston rotation; floor is a long reliever whose fastball at 94.0 mph plays better in shorter bursts.

reports.name: Trevor Megill
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.51 and the xwOBA at .248, both at the 97th percentile, which means the current ERA isn't running ahead of the underlying performance — the dominance is holding up in the shape of his contact. A 32.1% strikeout rate pairs with a 36.5% chase rate, and hitters are doing almost nothing with what they do manage to put in play: average exit velocity of 90.8 mph is well below most relievers you'd trust in high-leverage spots. The projection, 21 saves and a 3.26 ERA over 63.63 innings, is conservative relative to what the Statcast profile says he actually is right now, and the only real lever is whether Milwaukee keeps feeding him save situations rather than deploying him earlier in games. If the role holds, he's a legitimate closer with back-end impact; if they move him around, the counting stats soften but the pitcher stays exactly as dangerous.

reports.name: Thayron Liranzo
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 201 PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing here. Liranzo is drawing free passes at a 17% clip across AA and A ball, which translates to an 11.6% MLB-equivalent rate when the league average sits at 8.5%, and that discipline is what's propping up a .363 OBP despite a .237 average. Nine home runs in 223 PA suggest real raw pop, and the translated ISO of .151 lands right at MLB average, so the power is at least plausible at the next level even if it won't carry him there on its own. The problem is contact: a 26% strikeout rate in the minors becomes 26.6% in translation, and everything hinges on whether a 22-year-old catcher can tighten that up enough for the hit tool to become functional rather than a drain on everything else. If the plate discipline holds and the swing-and-miss recedes even a little, you're looking at a backup catcher who gets on base; if it doesn't, the approach grades out as lovely theory.

reports.name: Justin Wrobleski
reports.published_report: The walk rate tells the story: 4.9% BB% puts him in the 96th percentile, and that control is the only reason a 17.3% strikeout rate and 19.2% whiff rate can support a rotation spot. Hitters are making loud contact when they connect, 44.6% hard-hit and 90.6 mph average exit velocity near the bottom of the league, so the margin for error is thin and entirely dependent on keeping the ball out of the zone on hitters' terms. The 3.49 ERA projection is optimistic relative to a 4.27 xERA; if his command slips even a tick, there's not enough swing-and-miss to compensate. What he is, if it holds, is a soft-contact artist who gets deep into games on guile and location, the 2447 rpm fastball spin giving him at least one weapon to explain why the walks stay low — but if that command regresses, what's left is a fifth starter with below-average stuff and nowhere to hide.

reports.published_report: The .449 OBP headlining a .998 OPS across 227 combined PA is the loudest thing in the file, and it sits at the 99th percentile against the hitter pool. The whole profile hinges on whether a catcher can get enough defensive reps at the MLB level to stay in the lineup, because the translated strikeout rate of 24.5% isn't comfortable for a backup and there's an 85% bench/platoon probability baked into the ceiling already. reports.name: Jeremy Peña
reports.published_report: The xBA of .297 at the 96th percentile is the loudest number in this profile, and it explains almost everything. Peña runs a 34.9% chase rate, exit velocity at 87.2 mph, and a 4.0% barrel rate, all bottom-third marks, yet his contact quality translates into hits at a rate barely anyone matches, because 29.1 ft/s sprint speed at the 92nd percentile turns weak contact into problems for infielders. The projection's .280/.339/.430 line is entirely believable as a result: not a slugger, just a fast shortstop who makes contact at an unusually high rate and steals 15 bases on top of it. The profile hinges on that speed staying intact; if it fades, the soft contact catches up to him and the batting average drifts toward what the exit velocity actually deserves.

If the speed converts in a real role, he's a bench outfielder who can steal 20; if a club can't find a way to hide the bat, he's roster filler.

reports.name: Bo Davidson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is impact over 283 PA.
reports.published_report: The .522 slugging at AA is doing real work here: 18 home runs in 283 plate appearances with an ISO of .251 translates to an MLB-equivalent .174 ISO, which clears the league-average bar by enough to matter for a center fielder. The power grade is the profile's engine, and the hit tool looks credible on a .271 average against a .294 BABIP, nothing inflated. What keeps this from being a bigger conversation is the walk rate, a 10% clip in the minor leagues that translates to a near-average 8.4% in the majors, and a 25.1% translated strikeout rate that already sits above league average, so the approach won't carry him if the contact slips. The ceiling here is a low-end everyday regular, but at 85% probability the most likely outcome is a bench or platoon role, and the honest version of that is a left-handed bat with real pop who profiles fine against righties and gets exposed in deeper looks.

reports.name: Trace Bright
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is mixed over 49.7 IP.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole problem. Across 69.4 innings at AA and AAA this year, Bright is running a 5.1 BB/9 that translates to 4.5 at the MLB level, well above the 3.2 major-league average, and it's dragging a 1.6 WHIP and 6.80 ERA into territory that makes the strikeout rate irrelevant. The K/9 at 10.0 translates almost exactly to the MLB average, so there's no swing-and-miss surplus to bail out the command; the K-BB% of 12% comes out to 11.1 in translation, below a league average of 13.5. If the walks tighten, he's a useful middle reliever or back-end depth arm, the kind of 49% shot ValuCast sees as a real outcome — but if the command profile is fixed, this is a 46% shot at pure depth, a guy who lives on a 40-man roster until he doesn't.

If it does come, there's a useful arm here, maybe a reliever where the miss plays up in shorter stints, but the 61% projection toward "useful MLB arm" lives entirely on that conditional.

reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 61.3 IP.
reports.published_report: Thirteen-point-one strikeouts per nine at Single-A is loud, and the 3.70 ERA across 61.3 innings suggests it's translating into results, but the walk rate is where this profile fractures. reports.published_report: The power reads fine in AAA, 10 home runs and .188 ISO in 285 PA, but the MLB-equivalent translation shows it landing at exactly league average, which means the bat needs something else to carry it. That something else isn't there: a 31% strikeout rate in the minors becomes a projected 28.9% against big-league pitching, nearly seven points above what hitters face up there on average, and the walk rate barely moves at 8.6% translated. The hit tool and approach both grade 35, so the contact and on-base problems aren't a slump; they're the shape of the profile. If the power grades up as he climbs, he's a bench bat who earns a spot; if the strikeout rate holds where it is, the ISO alone won't be enough.

reports.name: Lucas Braun
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is mixed over 43.7 IP.
reports.published_report: The walk rate carries the argument here: 2.7 BB/9 in the minors translates to 3.0 at the MLB level, and that command grade sits at 65 on the skill shape. Everything else is more complicated. His 7.4 K/9 lands in the 11th percentile of this pitcher pool, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts strikeout rate at 7.2 — well below the MLB average of 8.6, a gap wide enough to matter once hitters can wait him out. The ERA (3.90, 69th percentile) and WHIP (1.40, 60th percentile) look presentable across 73.4 combined AA/AAA innings, but run prevention built on command rather than swing-and-miss has a ceiling, and that ceiling here is a useful MLB arm in 85% of outcomes with almost no path to a rotation spot. If the command holds at the next level he's a viable depth piece; if hitters lay off his stuff, there isn't a strikeout tool to fall back on.

reports.name: Jakob Wright
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 50 IP.
reports.published_report: Eleven strikeouts per nine innings at A+ is loud enough to make you look twice, but 40 walks in 50 innings will drown that out fast. The MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout rate right at league average, 8.5 against 8.6, while his walk rate translates to 5.9 against a major-league average of 3.2, and that gap is why a 65-grade miss tool produces a 40-grade dominance grade and a 5.4 ERA on the actual ledger. If the command ever tightens into a workable zone, there's a useful MLB arm here, the projection puts 52% weight on that outcome, but if it doesn't, he's the 43% version: a depth arm absorbing innings in the upper minors.

reports.name: Jack Cebert
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is bat missing over 49.7 IP.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the story here. A 2.3 BB/9 across 68 innings between A+ and AA translates to a projected 2.8 at the MLB level, below a league average that sits at 3.2, and the 93rd-percentile command grade reflects that shape cleanly. The strikeout rate is fine, not loud, and the translation to 8.4 K/9 against a major-league average of 8.6 confirms he's working the edges of competence rather than missing bats at volume. What makes this profile function is the combination: a K-BB% that translates to 14.2% against a 13.5% baseline means the walks he doesn't issue are doing real work, covering for strikeout stuff that won't carry a full rotation. The ceiling, honestly, is a useful arm, somewhere between a fifth starter and a reliable middle-relief option, and it hinges entirely on whether that command holds once opposing hitters have quality looks at his stuff.
